title: Marcus Garvey: Black Moses
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile Marcus Garvey, the Jamaican-born Pan-Africanist who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) and promoted back-to-Africa ideas. They cover his Jamaica and Costa Rica years, time in London, marriages to Amy Ashwood and Amy Jacques, UNIA growth in Harlem, the Black Star Line shipping company and its failure, the mail fraud conviction and deportation to Jamaica, J. Edgar Hoover's infiltration and harassment, the 1919 shooting, his meeting with a KKK leader, his death in London, and his legacy in Rastafarianism and reggae. The episode closes with listener mail correcting the census name of Reverend Kimple's wife.

segments.title: Introduction and overview of Marcus Garvey
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Marcus Garvey as a polarizing, influential Black activist tied to reggae and Rastafarianism, and preview his complicated legacy. They discuss his Jamaican birth, his parents, his early printing career, his years in Costa Rica, and his time in London where he encountered Pan-Africanism.

segments.title: Marriages and personal life
segments.summary: They cover Garvey's marriage to Amy Ashwood, the bitter divorce, and her role in founding UNIA. They also cover his later marriage to Amy Jacques, who had been Ashwood's friend, and her work for the movement and its newspaper page.

segments.title: Founding of UNIA and rise in Harlem
segments.summary: Garvey founds the Universal Negro Improvement Association, inspired by Booker T. Washington and Tuskegee, arriving in New York in 1916 after Washington's death. UNIA grows from a small Harlem basement chapter to a large worldwide movement, with membership claims the hosts consider inflated. Its appeal to Black veterans and working-class people after World War I is discussed.

segments.title: Garveyism, community programs, and symbols
segments.summary: The hosts describe Garveyism as a blend of American self-reliance and Black demands for equality, the UNIA's social programs and conferences, the Black Cross Nurses, the slogan 'Up you Mighty Race', and the Pan-African flag's red, green, and black colors. Garvey's flamboyant dress and title of Provisional President of Africa are also covered.

segments.title: Back to Africa movement origins
segments.summary: The hosts trace the back-to-Africa idea from Paul Cuffe's voyages and the American Colonization Society's Liberia project. They contrast it with Black Americans who felt rooted in America, and note Garvey's insistence that the races should not mix.

segments.title: Black Star Line and business troubles
segments.summary: The Black Star Line is founded in 1919 as a shipping company, financed by five-dollar shares sold to working-class families. The ships were in poor repair, the company was mismanaged, and Garvey's ventures, including the Negro Factories Corporation, were shuffled financially. Garvey's stops on shipping routes to sell shares are described.

segments.title: Mail fraud conviction, prison, and deportation
segments.summary: Federal authorities charged Garvey with mail fraud for promoting ships the company did not yet own. He was sentenced to five years, served about two, had his sentence commuted by Calvin Coolidge, and was deported to Jamaica. His health problems and overambition are discussed.

segments.title: Hoover surveillance, 1919 shooting, and final years
segments.summary: J. Edgar Hoover's infiltration of the movement through moles, including James Wormley Jones, and sabotage of Black Star Line fuel are covered. The October 1919 shooting by George Tyler is described, with Amy Ashwood reportedly shielding him. Garvey's later years, his death in London at 52, his criticism of Haile Selassie, his praise of Mussolini, and his meeting with a KKK leader are discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail and Garvey legacy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Garvey's rehabilitation by Rastafarians and his legacy, the PBS American Experience documentary, and a Winston Duke film. Listener Sue then provides census information identifying Reverend Kimple's wife as Eunice Kimple from the 1950 census.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with the show credits.
